title: CARS skills

Covers the user's IDs 8A (CARS foundations), 8B (Reasoning Within Text) and 8C (Reasoning Beyond Text). AAMC tests CARS by these three skills, not by content categories. By AAMC's published breakdown, Foundations of Comprehension is about 30% of CARS questions, Reasoning Within the Text about 30%, and Reasoning Beyond the Text about 40%.

A) HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY

  • Format: 53 questions, 90 minutes, 9 passages (humanities and social sciences). No outside knowledge is needed; everything must be supported by the passage.
  • Foundations of Comprehension: main idea, author's purpose and tone, meaning of words or phrases in context, what a paragraph contributes, and what the author implies but does not state.
  • Reasoning Within the Text: how claims relate to evidence; whether a claim is supported, assumed or contradicted; how parts of the argument fit; identifying the author's opinions vs. those the author reports.
  • Reasoning Beyond the Text: apply the passage's ideas to a new situation; judge how new information would strengthen, weaken or change the argument (it may fit, challenge, or require revising).
  • Passage mapping: one short note per paragraph (its job in the argument), then a one-line thesis plus the author's tone. Watch for pivot words (however, yet, but), emphasis words (crucially, above all) and opinion markers (I argue, it seems).
  • Voices: track who says what. Authors often describe a view in order to reject it.
  • Answer choices: the right answer is supported by specific lines. Wrong answers are often too extreme ("always," "never," "proves"), out of scope, the opposite of the author's view, true but irrelevant to the question, or a distortion that mixes passage words with a wrong relationship.
  • Strengthen/weaken: identify the claim the question targets first, then find the choice that most directly affects the link between that claim and its evidence.
  • Pacing: about 10 minutes per passage (3–4 reading, 6–7 questions). Skip and return rather than stall on one item.
  • Practice volume beats tricks: review every wrong answer by naming its trap type.

B) FORMULAS + PATHWAYS

SkillQuestion stems that signal itWhat to do
Foundations"main idea," "primary purpose," "in context, the word … means," "the author implies"Match your thesis line; reread the sentence around the word
Within the Text"which claim is supported by evidence," "the author assumes," "which statement is the author's view"Find the claim, locate its support, separate author from other voices
Beyond the Text"if … were true," "which new finding would most challenge," "the author would most likely agree that a new case…"Extract the passage's principle and apply it to the new case

Pathway: answering any CARS question

C) COMMON TRAPS + 3 MCAT-STYLE Qs

Trap 1: Picking a choice because it is true in the real world. CARS rewards what the passage supports. A choice that is factually correct but not supported, or not relevant to the question, is wrong.

Trap 2: Confusing the author's voice with a view the author reports. An author may spend a paragraph describing a theory before rejecting it. Check whose view each sentence expresses.

Practice passage (original, written for 520 Quest):

Museums once treated restoration as a return to an object's "original" state, filling gaps so seamlessly that visitors could not tell new paint from old. Many conservators now reject that ideal. A restoration that hides itself, they argue, quietly replaces the past with the restorer's guess about it. The newer practice of visible retouching—hatching in a missing area with fine lines that blend at a distance but separate up close—asks viewers to accept a work as damaged and survived rather than whole. Critics reply that such marks distract from the image and impose a modern scholarly taste on works made for devotion or delight. Yet this objection assumes that the viewer's first impression matters more than the viewer's knowledge of what is actually there. An honest repair, I would suggest, is not a lesser kind of beauty but a different and more truthful one.

Q1 (Foundations). The author's primary purpose is to:

  • A) describe the history of museum restoration techniques
  • B) defend visible retouching as more honest than seamless restoration
  • C) argue that damaged artworks should not be restored at all
  • D) show that critics of visible retouching misunderstand devotional art

Answer: B. The final sentence states the author's view: honest, visible repair is "more truthful."

  • A is wrong: the history is background for an argument, not the purpose.
  • B is correct.
  • C is wrong: too extreme; the author favors a kind of restoration, not none.
  • D is wrong: the author answers the critics' assumption about first impressions, not their understanding of devotional art.

Q2 (Within the Text). The critics' objection, as the author presents it, depends on which assumption?

  • A) Visible retouching damages the original paint
  • B) A viewer's immediate visual experience should take priority
  • C) Conservators should not have scholarly training
  • D) Seamless restoration is cheaper

Answer: B. The author says the objection "assumes that the viewer's first impression matters more than the viewer's knowledge."

  • A is wrong: the passage never claims physical damage.
  • B is correct.
  • C is wrong: "scholarly taste" is mentioned, but nothing about training.
  • D is wrong: cost is never discussed.

Q3 (Beyond the Text). Which new practice would the author most likely approve of?

  • A) Digitally removing cracks from a photograph of a fresco before printing it in a guidebook, without comment
  • B) Rebuilding a missing statue arm in a matching marble so the repair cannot be detected
  • C) Displaying a repaired vase with its new sections in a slightly lighter clay that is visible on close inspection
  • D) Refusing to display any damaged objects

Answer: C. It parallels visible retouching: it blends from afar but is honest up close.

  • A is wrong: it hides damage, which the author calls replacing the past with a guess.
  • B is wrong: undetectable repair is the ideal the author rejects.
  • C is correct.
  • D is wrong: the author values showing works as "damaged and survived."

More in the 5,180 Qbank: Full CARS passages with 5–6 questions each, for example passage #xp082 "Legible Hands" (visible retouching), #xp001 "Instruments That Argue", #xp046 "The Instructed Child" and #xp091 "The Unfair Persuader" (100 passages, xp001–xp100).
